THEMATIC AREA Environment, Wildlife and Natural Resources
Developers of forestry assets have to state how much carbon their trees store and how quickly it grows. Most estimate this from tape-measure plot surveys and spreadsheet projections. On projects of 10,000 hectares and above, that method is slow and uncertain. The uncertainty limits how much future carbon removal developers can commit to buyers. GAIA-M (Geospatial AI for Afforestation Monitoring) gives each project site its own biomass model. The model combines satellite imagery with drone LiDAR (laser scanning) and field measurements to map above-ground biomass and state the uncertainty of each estimate, for example 10,000 tonnes of CO2 removed, plus or minus 880 tonnes within a 95% interval. The project takes Treeconomy’s biomass model from project-by-project delivery to a production service that can assess whole forest portfolios, and tests the results with pilot users against their field data. The project targets less than 10% variance against ground-truth measurements on 95% of test plots, monitoring costs more than 60% below manual survey, and audit-ready reports within five working days for a 10,000 hectare project.
Project developers are the pilot users. Great Yellow (United Kingdom) and Wilderway (Netherlands, with restoration projects in the UK, Spain, Ireland and Portugal) provide site access and ground-truth data, and take part in requirements workshops. Natural capital asset managers are the licensing customers. Gresham House (United Kingdom) supplies portfolio-level reporting requirements. The project team’s initial understanding of user needs:
Monitoring cost per hectare well below manual plot surveys
Biomass estimates for the whole project area, with stated uncertainty
Evidence and validation that carbon standards bodies and independent verifiers accept
Reporting turnaround of days instead of months
Enough confidence in projected removals to commit more volume to offtake contracts
The main challenge for the project team is accuracy across contrasting sites, from mature woodland to bare ground, at the level a verifier requires. Field data also arrives in a different format from every user, and Treeconomy still prepares much of it by hand.
GAIA-M gives a project developer or asset manager a biomass map of the whole project site, with a stated uncertainty for every map cell and for the site total. Users open the results in a web browser, restyle maps, read exact values by hovering over a point, and download maps, statistics and audit-ready reports. The system works in three steps. Satellite images give regular coverage of the whole site. Drone laser scans (LiDAR) and field plots, where trees are measured on the ground, show what the satellite signal means in tonnes of biomass, and an AI model learns this link for each site. The model then propagates and estimates biomass everywhere on the site and reports how far each estimate may be from the true value. The system and the users site-specific model is accessed through Sherwood, Treeconomy’s web platform. An order starts an automated processing chain on Google Cloud, which runs the model and stores the results in cloud storage, where maps are drawn on request. Every run records the data and model versions it used, so a verifier can trace any figure to its inputs. A field data application, developed in the project, lets users add plot measurements to retune the model.
The project uses Sentinel-2 imagery from the Copernicus programme for regular coverage of every site, Sentinel-1 SAR, GEDI and ICESat spaceborne LiDAR, alongside commercial very high resolution imagery and additional satellite-derived products. The usual alternatives for monitoring biomass fall short on sites of 10,000 to 100,000 hectares. Manual plot surveys are accurate where they sample but cannot cover a site this size or be repeated cheaply each year. Satellite-only biomass maps cover everything but carry large uncertainty in varied woodland, with very high coefficients of variation commonly at project scale, too wide for institutional investors or large carbon purchase contracts. Combining the two provides the coverage and history of satellites with the accuracy of measured trees. The drone LiDAR and field plots are also what make a stated uncertainty possible. No competitors combine satellite, drone and field data for a single site and report the uncertainty.
The project started on 21 September 2026. The first month covered an audit of the existing biomass modelling code, interviews with prospective users and the business plan. Four UK sites totalling about 1,600 hectares are ready for data collection. They include mature and ancient woodland, young plantations and sites with very little vegetation. Field data collection is scheduled for the coming weeks, weather permitting. The project team is building a biomass pipeline to run at scale, with the aim of producing dozens of models in days where one model currently takes a few weeks. The next milestone, the Critical Design Review, requires a demonstration of an end-to-end example.
